passage:
Dear Indu,

I am writing from Melbourne, where I came for a conference and to stay with Nisha, my old college friend. Nisha lives alone, pays for a home carer for her mother, and visits her only twice a year. At first I found it lonely: a quiet flat, dinner for one, and I kept thinking of our house with five people talking at once. But when Nisha talks about her work and how nobody plans her weekends for her, her face lights up. She told me the distance is the price of the life she chose, and some days she is not sure it is a fair price. I still cannot imagine living like that. I will try not to read her life as cold.

Tell Mummy I will call on Sunday.

Alka

qa.q: Where is Alka writing the letter from?
qa.a: Alka is writing from Melbourne.

qa.q: What did Alka feel about Nisha's quiet flat at first?
qa.a: Alka found it lonely, missing the noisy house with five people talking at once.

qa.q: What could Alka do to see Nisha's life more fairly?
qa.a: Alka could keep listening to Nisha's own reasons and notice the parts that give Nisha joy, instead of reading the quiet as coldness.

qa.q: How does Nisha herself see her way of life?
qa.a: Nisha values planning her own weekends and calls the distance the price of the life she chose, though some days she is not sure it is a fair price.

grounding: A person from a close family culture finds friends' solitary life abroad lonely, yet sees the freedom those friends value.

passage:
Thanks for having me, Sachin. I'm Chandrika. You asked what surprised me on my trip to Toronto. I went to visit Marcus, a friend from my exchange year. His father lives back in Ohio with a paid home helper, and Marcus sees him twice a year. I was ready to feel sorry for him: a small flat, takeaway dinner, an empty calendar on Sundays. Where I come from, we would have called that lonely, and honestly, in the first two days I did.
Then I saw him on a video call with his father at eight sharp, laughing about a crossword. He told me he loves that no one decides his weekends, and that he still worries some nights about being far away. I went home still preferring my noisy family dinners. But I stopped calling his life cold.

qa.q: Where did Chandrika go to visit Marcus?
qa.a: Chandrika went to Toronto to visit Marcus.

qa.q: What did Chandrika feel about Marcus's small flat in the first two days?
qa.a: Chandrika felt sorry for him and found it lonely, the way it would have been called back where Chandrika comes from.

qa.q: How did seeing the video call change Chandrika's view?
qa.a: Chandrika saw Marcus laughing with his father at eight sharp and hearing that he loves deciding his own weekends, so Chandrika stopped calling his life cold while keeping a preference for noisy family dinners.

qa.q: What is it like for Marcus to live far from his father?
qa.a: Marcus enjoys that no one decides his weekends, but he also worries some nights about being far away, so he feels freedom and worry together.

grounding: A person from a close family culture sees a friend living alone far from an elder and finds it lonely, yet sees the freedom he values.

passage:
I shared a flat in London with Tanvir and Aadhya for a year, and I watched Tanvir slowly change his mind about something.
Aadhya grew up here. Her mother lives in a care home in Leeds, and Aadhya visits once a month, on a Sunday, and pays part of the fees. The first time Tanvir heard this, he went quiet. Later he said to me, "In Dhaka, my grandmother lives with us. We'd never put her in a home. It feels so lonely."
But over the months he saw other things. Aadhya called her mother every evening. She'd chosen her own degree, her own city, her own partner, and nobody had fought her about it. Tanvir once admitted his uncles still decide his cousins' weddings.
One night he said, "Maybe she's lonelier than we'd be. But she's also freer." I don't know exactly what he felt. But he started calling his grandmother more often.

qa.q: How often does Aadhya visit her mother?
qa.a: Aadhya visits once a month, on a Sunday.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have been feeling when he went quiet?
qa.a: Tanvir probably felt sad and uneasy, since in his family an elder would never be put in a home, and it seemed lonely to him.

qa.q: What did Tanvir come to notice over the year?
qa.a: He saw that Aadhya stayed close through daily calls and had freedom to choose her degree, city and partner, which his family's way can limit.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see her own family life?
qa.a: Aadhya probably sees it as caring and normal, with daily calls and monthly visits, and values the freedom she has.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young man from a close family culture find his friend's independent family life lonely, and slowly see the freedom it offers.

passage:
First month. Ishita, twenty-four, newly arrived in Berlin from Pune, learned that her colleague Hafsa lived alone and saw her parents twice a year, though they lived an hour away. "That's so cold," Ishita told her mother on the phone. "Nobody here eats together."
Third month. Hafsa invited Ishita for coffee. She told her about moving out at eighteen, choosing art school over her father's wishes, and paying her own rent since then. "My parents and I are closer now than when I lived there," she said. Ishita was surprised.
Sixth month. Ishita got a promotion. Her family's first question was when she'd return to marry. She felt the familiar squeeze in her chest. That evening she told Hafsa, "I used to think your life was lonely. Maybe it is, a bit. But you've never had to ask permission to be yourself." Hafsa laughed. "And you've never eaten Christmas dinner alone."

qa.q: How often did Hafsa see her parents?
qa.a: Hafsa saw her parents twice a year.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when her family asked when she'd return to marry?
qa.a: Ishita felt pressured and hemmed in, a familiar squeeze in her chest.

qa.q: What helped Ishita see Hafsa's life more fairly?
qa.a: Talking with Hafsa over coffee let Ishita hear how independence brought her freedom and a closer relationship with her parents.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Ishita's close family life?
qa.a: Hafsa seems to see its warmth, since she points out that Ishita has never eaten Christmas dinner alone.

grounding: Over months abroad, a young woman from a close family culture sees a colleague's independent life as lonely, then recognises the freedom it gives.

passage:
Chetan, you think the Americans are cold because your manager didn't come to your father's funeral? Let me tell you about my years in Chicago.
I was twenty-five, fresh from Kanpur. My landlady was eighty and lived alone. Her son lived three streets away and visited on Sundays, with a pie. I was horrified. "Three streets!" I told my mother on the phone. "He should live with her!"
One winter, the landlady fell on the ice. I carried her groceries for weeks. One evening she told me, "My son wanted me to move in. I refused. I raised three children in that kitchen. Now it's my kitchen. I like my freedom."
I didn't understand then. I do now. When my own sons tried to decide everything for me after my surgery, I remembered her.
So, Chetan, maybe it's lonelier there. But it's also freer. Suraj Nana is telling you: both have a price.

qa.q: How often did the landlady's son visit?
qa.a: Her son visited on Sundays, with a pie.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when he first saw the landlady living alone?
qa.a: Suraj felt horrified, believing her son should live with her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Suraj's story?
qa.a: When the landlady explained that she refused to move in with her son because she valued her freedom, Suraj began to understand.

qa.q: How did the landlady see her own life?
qa.a: She saw it as free and hers, proud of her kitchen and her independence rather than lonely.

grounding: An elder recalls finding life abroad lonely when elders lived alone, then learning that those people valued freedom collectivist life can limit.

passage: The snowstorm cancelled Sudha's train out of Oslo, so she spent three extra days in her college friend Ramesh's tiny flat. He had lived there four years. His neighbour, Ingrid, eighty-one, lived alone next door; a paid carer came at ten and again at six. Her son phoned on Sundays and visited at Christmas. Sudha thought of her own Nani, who had never once eaten a meal alone. "Isn't it lonely?" she whispered to Ramesh. "Ask her," he said. So on the second evening, over cardamom buns, Sudha did. Ingrid laughed. "Lonely sometimes. But I choose my day. My son has his life; I had mine. Nobody tells me when to sleep." Sudha walked back through the snow, unsure. It still looked cold to her. It also looked free.

qa.q: How often does Ingrid's son phone and visit?
qa.a: Her son phones on Sundays and visits at Christmas.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she whispered "Isn't it lonely?"
qa.a: Sudha felt sad and a little uneasy, comparing Ingrid's life with her Nani's, who never ate a meal alone.

qa.q: What did Sudha do that helped her see past a stereotype?
qa.a: Instead of judging from outside, she asked Ingrid directly, and heard both the loneliness and the freedom Ingrid values.

qa.q: How does Ingrid see her own life?
qa.a: Ingrid admits she is sometimes lonely but values choosing her own day and letting her son live his own life.

grounding: It illustrates someone from a close family culture who finds an elder living alone abroad lonely, then hears the freedom that way of life prizes.
